records.sourceFile: Local heat therapy to accelerate recovery after exercise-induced muscle damage.pdf

paper.citation: Kim K, Monroe JC, Gavin TP, Roseguini BT. Local Heat Therapy to Accelerate Recovery After Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage. Exerc Sport Sci Rev. 2020;48(4):163-169.
paper.abstract: This review tests the hypothesis that local heat therapy speeds functional recovery after strenuous eccentric exercise by aiding glycogen resynthesis, reversing vascular dysfunction, improving mitochondrial function and stimulating muscle protein synthesis. The authors summarize cell, animal and human evidence and conclude that localized heating is a promising recovery tool that needs further study.
paper.tldr: Local heat therapy may speed recovery of muscle function after eccentric exercise through better blood flow, glycogen resynthesis and mitochondrial function. The mechanisms are mostly supported by non-athlete and cell or animal work, so they remain unproven in athletes.
paper.methods: This is a narrative review with no described literature search method. It organizes evidence from cultured cells, rodents, pigs and humans around heat-induced signaling, muscle blood flow, glycogen resynthesis, microvascular function, mitochondria, protein turnover and soreness.
paper.findings: In the authors' own earlier study (Kim et al., 2019), one thigh heated for 90 minutes immediately after maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise and daily for 4 days recovered fatigue resistance faster than the thermoneutral control thigh (main effect of treatment, P = 0.02), and soreness tended to resolve faster. Cited human studies report faster glycogen resynthesis with local heat after exhaustive cycling, and mechanistic studies show heat-related increases in muscle blood flow, eNOS, angiogenic factors and mitochondrial proteins, although one cited study found 20 minutes of 46 C leg immersion did not increase myofibrillar protein synthesis. The authors note the glycogen studies did not use eccentric exercise and that most human evidence comes from exercise-naive or recreationally active people.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so its coverage cannot be judged. Much of the evidence is from cell, rat, mouse and pig models, and the authors state it is unclear whether the findings apply to competitive athletes. The review also states that the optimal timing of heat (before or after exercise) is not yet defined and that effects on connective tissue repair are unexplored.
paper.practicalImplications: Localized heat is a possible recovery option after strenuous eccentric exercise, but the review does not establish a protocol, dose or timing for athletes. Staff should treat the proposed mechanisms as hypotheses and should not expect the same recovery gains in trained athletes until the authors' call for further study is answered.
paper.athleteDev: Heat therapy may be considered as a recovery aid after high-volume eccentric training, but the review does not show that it improves later training adaptation or competitive performance. Its proposed effects on glycogen and mitochondria come mainly from non-athlete or non-eccentric studies.
paper.rtp: The review discusses recovery after muscle damage in general and does not assess return-to-sport decisions or injured athletes. It cannot be used to judge readiness to return to sport, though it notes heat is used in sports rehabilitation settings.

records.sourceFile: Managing travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes - A review and consensus statement.pdf

paper.citation: Janse van Rensburg DC, Jansen van Rensburg A, Fowler PM, Bender AM, Stevens D, Sullivan KO, et al. Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes: A Review and Consensus Statement. Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: The authors review circadian physiology, travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes, and give consensus recommendations for managing both. The recommendations are organized as travel toolboxes for pre-flight, in-flight and post-flight phases, with the authors noting that research is needed to strengthen them.
paper.tldr: Travel fatigue and jet lag can affect sleep, performance and illness risk, but evidence for specific management is limited. The panel's toolbox favors protecting sleep, planning recovery windows, timed light exposure and avoidance, and sensible melatonin use, with caution about unvalidated tools.
paper.methods: Expert panel of 26 that ran literature searches in PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Google Scholar and SPORTDiscus, then used Qualtrics voting on terminology, travel fatigue management and jet lag management. Consensus thresholds were 80% for terminology and travel fatigue and 75% for jet lag, with average author response rates of 96.2% and 92.3%.
paper.findings: The authors report no research on interventions that specifically manage travel fatigue in athletes, and a cited systematic review found low-quality evidence for jet lag interventions. Consensus recommendations include protecting sleep before and during travel, timed light exposure and avoidance, and exogenous melatonin, with the authors noting that inappropriate light exposure can be counterproductive. The authors caution against jet lag calculators and apps until their efficacy in athletes is tested.
paper.limitations: The recommendations rest mainly on opinion, collective experience and laboratory or community studies rather than athlete trials, and the authors say this limits the strength of recommendation. The extracted text does not include the content of Table 4 or the figure dosing schedules, so specific timing advice could not be checked against the source.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan training load and recovery around travel so athletes have time to adjust, and protect sleep before and during long journeys. Use the light and melatonin guidance only with individual supervision, because the authors say inappropriate light can be counterproductive and app-based timing advice is unvalidated.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the toolbox to plan training load and recovery windows around travel, and can track sleep and fatigue with subjective tools such as the Total Quality of Recovery scale. The authors say no single marker captures travel fatigue, so these are monitoring aids rather than performance tests.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address return to sport after injury. Its guidance applies to fit, travelling athletes, and it should not be used to make return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Medications for Sleep Schedule              Adjustments in Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Baird MB, Asif IM. Medications for sleep schedule adjustments in athletes. Sports Health. 2018;10(1):35-39.
paper.abstract: The authors review evidence for melatonin, caffeine and nonbenzodiazepine sleep aids used to shift athletes' sleep schedules around travel and competition. They give timing recommendations for sports medicine providers and note that most supporting data come from non-athlete populations.
paper.tldr: Melatonin, caffeine and nonbenzodiazepine sleep aids may help athletes shift sleep schedules, but very few studies test them in athletes. Most guidance comes from shift workers and travellers, so timing should be individualised and checked against anti-doping rules.
paper.methods: Clinical review using MEDLINE keyword searches on sleep aids, circadian adjustment, athletes, caffeine and melatonin. The authors extracted and discussed pertinent articles, with no stated inclusion criteria, and assigned a level of evidence of 2.
paper.findings: Melatonin is presented as the best-studied agent, with benefits for sleep phase advancement such as eastward travel and early competition. Early-day caffeine may help re-entrainment and alertness, but caffeine taken for late afternoon or evening competitions may impair sleep. Sedative-hypnotics are described as second-line agents for phase advance, with short-acting agents preferred, benzodiazepines discouraged, and at least 8 hours of sleep advised before competition. In a trial of 12 soccer players, morning melatonin reduced physical performance at 08:00 with no differences at 12:00 or 16:00, and a second athlete trial found no likely effect on morning performance after night-time melatonin.
paper.limitations: The review uses a keyword MEDLINE search with no inclusion criteria, and the authors state that few studies involve athletes. Much of the guidance is inferred from shift workers, aircrew and other travellers, and caffeine tolerance was not adjusted for in the cited studies. The cited soccer trial's authors concluded morning melatonin had no unfavourable effects even though performance fell at 08:00.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports medicine providers can time melatonin to the direction of travel as the review's table sets out, and use sedative-hypnotics only when at least 8 hours of sleep is available before preparation and competition. The review accepts caffeine shortly before competition for its ergogenic effect, but staff should weigh its cost to sleep after late afternoon or evening events. Melatonin supplements and energy drinks are not regulated to prescription standards, so contamination and anti-doping risk should be checked, and the authors note ramelteon as a prescription alternative.
paper.athleteDev: Plan sleep timing, naps and light exposure around travel and competition before turning to medication, as the review recommends non-drug strategies first. Any sleep aid plan should be individualised, because the authors note that each athlete's circadian physiology differs.
paper.rtp: The review addresses sleep schedules and jet lag, not injury, so it cannot inform return to sport. It should not be used to decide when an injured athlete can return to training or competition.

records.sourceFile: Multidimensional Monitoring of        Recovery Status and Implications for Performance.pdf

paper.citation: Heidari J, Beckmann J, Bertollo M, Brink M, Kallus W, Robazza C, et al. Multidimensional Monitoring of Recovery Status and Implications for Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018.
paper.abstract: This invited brief review describes recovery monitoring in athletes across biological, psychological and social approaches. It argues that these approaches should be combined rather than relying on a single measure, and that monitoring should use individual reference values.
paper.tldr: Recovery monitoring should combine biological, psychological and social tools rather than rely on one measure, with individual baselines and the smallest meaningful change used to judge results. The review does not test these recommendations, so treat them as a framework.
paper.methods: Invited brief review; the article does not describe a literature search, study selection or quality appraisal. It summarizes biological markers (resting HRV, heart rate recovery, creatine kinase, testosterone/cortisol ratio, immune markers), psychological questionnaires (MTDS, POMS and BRUMS, RESTQ-Sport and RESTQ-Sport-36, ARSS and SRSS) and a social stress tool (DALDA).
paper.findings: The authors suggest combining five minutes of resting HRV with submaximal exercise heart rate as the most feasible cardiac measures, but say the response to underrecovery is hard to generalize across sports. They state that no single biological marker is a gold standard, that links between hormones and performance are weak, and they cite a testosterone/cortisol ratio drop of more than 30% as a sign of overtraining from one older source. They recommend a multimodal approach with individual reference values, the smallest meaningful change, and key assessments at set points combined with brief regular checks.
paper.limitations: This narrative review has no described search or quality appraisal, so its claims cannot be checked against a defined evidence base. The authors note that no consensus exists on the optimal biological parameter, that biological markers vary widely between and within athletes, and that the logistics of blood sampling limit daily use.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff setting up recovery monitoring should choose tools by goal and time budget: the review suggests key assessments at set points, such as preseason and postseason, with brief regular measures such as the MTDS between them. Judge changes against each athlete's own reference values and the smallest meaningful change, and use blood or saliva markers only where laboratory turnaround and resources allow.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports combining a few brief self-report measures with periodic fuller assessments and individual baselines to detect changes in recovery. It also says the link between hormonal markers and performance is weak, so its performance-related advice is a framework rather than tested evidence.
paper.rtp: The review covers recovery monitoring in athletes and does not address injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. Its note that RESTQ-Sport includes an injury scale and that underrecovery can precede injury does not give return-to-play criteria, so it should not be used to clear an athlete to return.

records.sourceFile: Napping behavior, daytime sleepiness, and arousal in high performance athletes and non-athlete controls.pdf

paper.citation: Pereira R, Hartescu I, Jackson RC, Morgan K. Napping behaviour, daytime sleepiness, and arousal in high performance athletes and non-athlete controls. J Sports Sci. 2023.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional online survey of 158 high-performance athletes and 82 non-athlete controls to examine napping in relation to sleep quality, daytime sleepiness and pre-sleep arousal. Athlete and non-athlete nap prevalence did not differ significantly, and athletes had longer self-reported sleep and lower cognitive arousal. Among athletes, higher daytime sleepiness was associated with napping (OR 4.91), and each point higher on cognitive arousal was associated with lower odds of napping (OR 0.95).
paper.tldr: Athletes nap about as often as active non-athletes, and napping among athletes is linked to daytime sleepiness and lower pre-sleep cognitive arousal rather than to poorer night sleep. About half of athletes did not nap, and many non-nappers said napping would hurt their night sleep or that they could not fall asleep when they tried.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics) of athletes at least semi-elite and non-athlete controls who were active at WHO activity levels but not competitive. Measures included the PSQI, Pre-sleep Arousal Scale, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, GAD-7, FIRST and rMEQ, plus single items on napping. Analyses used age-adjusted ANCOVA, chi-square and logistic regression in SPSS 27.
paper.findings: Nap prevalence was 51.3% in athletes and 36.6% in non-athletes, a non-significant age-adjusted difference (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.35-1.13). Athletes had longer self-reported total sleep time (456 vs 419 minutes, p<0.001) and lower cognitive arousal, but PSQI global scores did not differ. Among athletes, higher daytime sleepiness predicted napping (OR 4.91, 95% CI 2.38-10.13) and each 1-point rise in cognitive arousal lowered the odds of napping (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-0.99); in the combined athlete and non-athlete sample, nappers with lower sleepiness had lower cognitive arousal than non-nappers (difference 4.2 points, p=.005). Team and individual sport athletes had similar nap prevalence (51.9% vs 50.6%), but individual sport athletes had higher somatic and cognitive arousal and higher sleep reactivity.
paper.limitations: The sample was recruited through convenience methods and was not random, and women were over-represented. The authors note the large number of comparisons, though they used Bonferroni post-hoc tests. The Discussion gives the female share of athletes as 61.7% while Table 1 gives 64.6%, the team (76) and individual (80) groups sum to 156 rather than 158, and the single napping item and self-report measures limit what the data can show.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not assume that athletes who avoid napping have adequate night sleep, because about half of athletes in this sample did not nap, many non-nappers gave a concern about night sleep as their reason, and non-nappers reported lower daytime sleepiness. Before recommending a planned nap, staff could ask athletes about daytime sleepiness and whether they can fall asleep in the day, then monitor the effect on night sleep.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the findings suggest that nap programs should account for individual differences in sleepiness and arousal, rather than assuming all athletes will benefit. Individual sport athletes in this sample reported higher arousal and sleep reactivity, so they may need different support for daytime sleep.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation and included no injured athletes. Its nap and sleepiness findings should not be used to judge readiness to return to training or competition.

records.sourceFile: Napping in high performance athletes sleepiness or sleepability.pdf

paper.citation: Gupta L, Morgan K, North C, Gilchrist S. Napping in high-performance athletes: sleepiness or sleepability? Eur J Sport Sci. 2020.
paper.abstract: Daytime napping in high-performance athletes is widely assumed to reflect sleepiness from sleep debt, but this has not been tested against a control group. In a two-trial laboratory study, elite (n=10), sub-elite (n=10) and non-athlete (n=10) participants had polysomnography-measured sleep latency during a single 20-minute nap opportunity. Elite athletes had shorter sleep latencies than controls on both trials, and Table 2 shows these elite differences remained significant after separate adjustment for 15:00 sleepiness and prior-night total sleep time; sub-elite results were less consistent, which the authors interpret as a gradient in sleepability.
paper.tldr: Elite athletes fell asleep faster than matched controls during a daytime nap opportunity, and this was not fully explained by how sleepy they felt. The authors suggest some athlete napping may reflect a capacity to sleep on demand rather than sleep debt, but the sample of 30 is small.
paper.methods: Two laboratory visits (adaptation and experimental trial) with a single polysomnography nap opportunity at 15:00 and a 20-minute maximum. Groups were elite and sub-elite athletes and active non-athlete controls recruited from a university population, with actigraphy screening for insomnia and sleep duration. Sleep latency and Karolinska Sleepiness Scale scores were compared using regression models adjusted for pre-trial sleepiness or total sleep time, with Fisher's exact tests for the proportion with high sleep tendency.
paper.findings: Elite athletes had shorter sleep latencies than controls in both trials (10.4 vs 16.3 minutes on the adaptation trial, p=0.02; 7.9 vs 13.7 minutes on the experimental trial, p=0.02), and Table 2 shows adjusted elite differences of about 6 minutes, all p<0.05. Sub-elite athletes had shorter latencies than controls on the adaptation trial (8.0 vs 16.3 minutes, p=0.001) but not significantly on the experimental trial (9.1 minutes, p=0.055 unadjusted; p=0.07 after adjustment for total sleep time). High sleep tendency (latency 8 minutes or less) was reached by 2, 8 and 5 of 10 controls, sub-elite and elite athletes in the adaptation trial and by 2, 6 and 8 of 10 in the experimental trial (both Fisher's exact p<0.05).
paper.limitations: Only 10 participants per group, and the authors note reduced power and unstable group means in the experimental trial; pre-trial training was not controlled. The abstract's 'all p<0.05' applies only to the elite group: the sub-elite TST-adjusted experimental difference was p=0.07 and the KSS-adjusted experimental model overall was p=0.07. Table 2 prints high-sleep-tendency percentages as shares of all high-tendency participants (for example 13.3%, 53.3%, 33.3%) rather than of each group of 10, and some adjusted confidence intervals are printed without negative signs.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not assume that a teammate who naps easily is sleep-deprived, since in this small study elite athletes fell asleep quickly without being sleepier than controls. The results suggest that athletes who settle quickly into a new sleep environment may cope better with travel and camps, but this needs replication before it is used to select or monitor athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not test performance, so its implications for training are indirect. It suggests that the ability to fall asleep on demand may differ between athletes, which could matter for nap scheduling around training loads, but the study does not show whether naps help performance.
paper.rtp: The study does not involve injured athletes, and it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Sleep latency during a lab nap should not be used to judge an injured athlete's recovery or readiness.

records.sourceFile: Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery after Heavy Resistance, Jump, and Sprint Training.pdf

paper.citation: Thomas K, Brownstein CG, Dent J, Parker P, Goodall S, Howatson G. Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery after Heavy Resistance, Jump, and Sprint Training. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018;50(12):2526-2535.
paper.abstract: In 10 male athletes, heavy-resistance, jump and sprint sessions performed with maximal intent produced neuromuscular fatigue that took up to 72 hours to resolve. Potentiated twitch force remained reduced for 48 hours after all sessions, and voluntary activation was reduced for 24 to 48 hours. The authors conclude that this fatigue is multifactorial and not primarily central.
paper.tldr: Heavy strength, jump and sprint sessions performed with maximal intent reduced maximal force and twitch force for 48 hours in ten male athletes, with recovery by 72 hours. Central fatigue recovered faster than peripheral fatigue, and the authors give partial support to separating such sessions by at least 48 hours when peak performance matters.
paper.methods: Crossover design in which 10 male athletes completed three sessions a week apart in randomized order: 10 sets of 5 back squats at 80% 1RM, 10 sets of 5 jump squats, and 15 sprints of 30 m. Before, immediately after, and at 24, 48 and 72 hours, the authors measured maximal isometric force, voluntary activation, twitch force, corticospinal excitability and intracortical inhibition, plus soreness, perceived fatigue and creatine kinase.
paper.findings: All three sessions reduced maximal isometric force for 48 hours, with average decrements of 8% (strength), 7% (jump) and 6% (sprint), and values were back to baseline at 72 hours. Potentiated quadriceps twitch force was reduced at 48 hours after every session, and was lower immediately after the strength session than after the jump and sprint sessions. Voluntary activation was reduced for 24 hours after jump and sprint sessions and for 48 hours after the strength session, while corticospinal excitability and intracortical inhibition did not change.
paper.limitations: The sessions could not be matched for training load, so between-session differences should be treated with caution, and the authors note that the jump session may have differed in muscle damage and work. The sample was small and all male, and the exercises were limited to high-volume sessions that may not reflect typical training. The authors also note that measurement tools for central fatigue have limited validity.
paper.practicalImplications: When peak performance is the priority, the authors give partial support to separating maximal-intent strength, jump or sprint sessions by at least 48 hours, since most measures took up to 72 hours to return to baseline. Monitoring should include peripheral and perceptual measures, because the authors found the residual fatigue to be multifactorial.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the time course (force and twitch deficits at 48 hours, recovered by 72 hours; perceived fatigue raised for 24 hours after jumps and 48 hours after strength and sprints; soreness raised for 48 hours) when planning maximal-intent lower-body sessions. Because the study used high-volume, single-exercise sessions, these timings should not be applied directly to varied programs.
paper.rtp: The study uses healthy trained men and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. Its fatigue timeline may inform load planning, but it should not be used for return-to-play or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Night Games and Sleep- Physiological, Neuroendocrine, and Psychometric Mechanisms.pdf

paper.citation: Juliff LE, Peiffer JJ, Halson SL. Night Games and Sleep: Physiological, Neuroendocrine, and Psychometric Mechanisms. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: In 12 netball athletes, sleep after a night game was shorter, less efficient and ended earlier than sleep on a time-matched rest day. Adrenaline and noradrenaline were higher around the game, but they did not correlate with sleep, while higher trait hyperarousal was associated with lower sleep efficiency.
paper.tldr: After a 6 pm netball game, these 12 athletes slept less, woke earlier and had lower sleep efficiency than on a rest day. Catecholamine and cortisol changes did not track with the sleep loss, but higher trait hyperarousal was linked to poorer sleep efficiency.
paper.methods: Observational crossover design in 12 netball athletes, comparing an evening international game (6 pm start) with a time-matched rest day that took place 10 days later. Sleep was monitored for two weeks with diaries and Actiware-scored wrist actigraphy. Measures included core temperature by ingestible telemetry pill, salivary cortisol at eight time points, 24-hour urinary adrenaline and noradrenaline, the Pre-Sleep Arousal Scale, the Karolinska Sleep Questionnaire, and a trait hyperarousal scale. Analysis used paired t tests, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Spearman correlations.
paper.findings: Compared with the rest day, the night game produced a shorter sleep duration (P = .02, d = 1.13), lower sleep efficiency (P < .001, d = 0.73) and earlier wake times (P <= .01, d = 0.959). Eleven of 12 athletes had objectively shorter sleep, with reductions of 15 to 140 minutes. Adrenaline (main effect P = .02) and noradrenaline (main effect P < .01) were higher across the game day, and cortisol was higher on the morning of the game, immediately after the game and one hour after it. Bedtime cortisol and bedtime core temperature did not differ between conditions. Trait hyperarousal was negatively correlated with sleep efficiency (rs = -0.611, P <= .01), while the catecholamine and cortisol measures were not correlated with sleep variables.
paper.limitations: Twelve athletes is a small convenience sample, which the authors acknowledge may limit significance. The rest day always followed the game by 10 days, so the order of conditions was not counterbalanced, and match-day load was not analysed. Inference: the hyperarousal correlation is reported with 23 degrees of freedom, which does not match 12 athletes, so the unit of analysis is unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan for shorter, lower-quality sleep after evening games, and build recovery time around the likely earlier wake-up. The authors suggest targeting hyperarousal in susceptible athletes, since higher trait scorers slept less efficiently. Bedtime cortisol and core temperature (about 3 hours after the game) and catecholamines did not correlate with sleep here, so they should not be used to predict post-game sleep.
paper.athleteDev: Evening competition shortened and reduced the quality of sleep in these netball athletes, which can cut into recovery between games in a tournament. The hyperarousal result suggests that athletes with higher trait arousal may need individual sleep support after night games. The findings come from one game in a small group and are not a basis for fixed training rules.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport after injury or illness, and it cannot be used to judge readiness to play. It describes sleep after a single night game in athletes who were in national age-group teams, so it may inform recovery planning after a late game, but not medical clearance.
